Agentic AI Patterns

Stop Prompting, Start Designing — 5 patterns that actually work

This is my personal copy of the article, turned into a lesson I can keep coming back to. Each chapter has the original text, the original illustration, a "Teach me" button that breaks the idea down conversationally, and a spot for me to write down what I actually learned.

  • Introduction→

  • 2. Tool Use→

Original article: "Stop Prompting, Start Designing: 5 Agentic AI Patterns That Actually Work" by Paolo Perrone. Diagrams: Avi Chawla.
Introduction

Why prompting alone wasn't enough

When I first started working with LLMs, I thought it was all about writing the perfect prompt. Feed it enough context and — boom — it should just work, right?

Not quite.

Early on, I realized I was basically tossing words at a glorified autocomplete. The output looked smart, but it didn't understand anything. It couldn't plan, adjust, or reason. One small phrasing tweak, and the whole thing broke.

What I was missing was structure. Intelligence isn't just about spitting out answers: it's about how those answers are formed. The process matters.

That's what led me to agentic AI patterns, design techniques that give LLMs a bit more intention. They let the model plan, reflect, use tools, even work with other agents. These patterns helped me go from brittle, hit-or-miss prompts to something that actually gets stuff done.

Here are the five patterns that made the biggest difference, explained in a way that's actually usable.

Pattern 1 of 5

Reflection: Teach Your Agent to Check Its Own Work

Ever asked ChatGPT a question, read the answer, and thought, "This sounds good… but something's off"?

That's where Reflection comes in. It's a simple trick: have the model take a second look at its own output before finalizing it.

The basic flow:

  1. Ask the question.
  2. Have the model answer.
  3. Then prompt it again: "Was that complete? Anything missing? How could it be better?"
  4. Let it revise itself.

You're not stacking models or adding complexity. You're just making it double-check its work. And honestly, that alone cuts down on a ton of sloppy mistakes; especially for code, summaries, or anything detail-heavy.

Think of it like giving your model a pause button and a mirror.
Pattern 2 of 5

Tool Use: Don't Expect the Model to Know Everything

Your LLM doesn't know what's in your database. Or your files. Or today's headlines. And that's okay — because you can let it fetch that stuff.

The Tool Use pattern connects the model to real-world tools. Instead of hallucinating, it can query a vector DB, run code in a REPL, or call external APIs like Stripe, WolframAlpha, or your internal endpoints.

This setup does require a bit of plumbing: function-calling, routing, maybe something like LangChain or Semantic Kernel, but it pays off. Your agent stops guessing and starts pulling real data.

People assume LLMs should be smart out of the box. They're not. But they get a lot smarter when they're allowed to reach for the right tools.

Pattern 3 of 5

ReAct: Let the Model Think While It Acts

Reflection's good. Tools are good. But when you let your agent think and act in loops, it gets even better.

That's what the ReAct pattern is all about: Reasoning + Acting.

Instead of answering everything in one go, the model reasons step-by-step and adjusts its actions as it learns more.

Example:

  • Goal: "Find the user's recent invoices."
  • Step 1: "Query payments database."
  • Step 2: "Hmm, results are outdated. Better ask the user to confirm."
  • Step 3: Adjust query, repeat.

It's not just responding — it's navigating.

To make ReAct work, you'll need three things:

  • Tools (for taking action)
  • Memory (for keeping context)
  • A reasoning loop (to track progress)

ReAct makes your agents flexible. Instead of sticking to a rigid script, they think through each step, adapt in real-time, and course-correct as new information comes in.

If you want to build anything beyond a quick one-off answer, this is the pattern you need.

Pattern 4 of 5

Planning: Teach Your Agent to Think Ahead

LLMs are pretty good at quick answers. But for anything involving multiple steps? They fall flat.

Planning helps with that.

Instead of answering everything in one shot, the model breaks the goal into smaller, more manageable tasks.

Let's say someone asks, "Help me launch a product." The agent might respond with:

  1. Define the audience
  2. Design a landing page
  3. Set up email campaigns
  4. Draft announcement copy

Then it tackles each part, one step at a time.

You can bake this into your prompt or have the model come up with the plan itself. Bonus points if you store the plan somewhere so the agent can pick up where it left off later.

Planning turns your agent from a reactive helper into a proactive one.

This is the pattern to use for workflows and any task that needs multiple steps.

Pattern 5 of 5

Multi-Agent: Get a Team Working Together

Why rely on one agent when you can have a whole team working together?

Multi-Agent setups assign different roles to different agents, each handling a piece of the puzzle. They collaborate — sometimes even argue — to come up with better solutions.

Typical setup:

  • Researcher gathers info
  • Planner outline steps
  • Coder writes the code
  • Reviewer double-check everything
  • PM: keeps it all moving

It doesn't have to be fancy. Even basic coordination works:

  • Give each agent a name and job.
  • Let them message each other through a controller.
  • Watch as they iterate, critique, and refine.

The magic happens when they disagree. That's when you get sharper insights and deeper thinking.

Putting it together

Want to Try This? Here's a Simple Starting Point

Let's say you're building a research assistant. Here's a no-nonsense setup that puts these patterns into play:

Start with Planning
Prompt: "Break this research task into clear steps before answering."
Example: "1. Define keywords, 2. Search recent papers, 3. Summarize findings."

Use Tool Use
Hook it up to a search API or a vector DB so it's pulling real facts — not making stuff up.

Add Reflection
After each answer, prompt: "What's missing? What could be clearer?" Then regenerate.

Wrap it in ReAct
Let the agent think between steps. "Results look shallow — retrying with new terms." Then act again.

Expand to Multi-Agent (optional)
One agent writes. Another critiques.
They talk. They argue. The output gets better.

That's it. You've got a working MVP. No fancy frameworks required, just smart prompts, basic glue code, and clear roles. You'll be surprised how much more LLM's confident you'll feel.

Closing thoughts

Wrapping Up

Agentic design isn't about making the model smarter. It's about designing better systems. Systems that manage complexity, adapt mid-flight, and don't fall apart at the first unexpected input.

These patterns helped reframe LLMs — not as magic boxes, but as messy components in a bigger process. They're not perfect. But they're powerful — if you give them structure.

Because the real intelligence? It's in the scaffolding you build around the model. Not just in the model itself.

The intelligence lives in the design, not just the model. And that's both frustrating and freeing.

Introduction

Background

Hello guys, welcome back to another exciting article on working with multi-agent AI systems. In this article, we'll dive into the basics of multi-agent architecture, we'll go over a couple of multi-agent architectures mainly:

  1. Single Agents
  2. Supervision
  3. Hierarchical
  4. Network
  5. Custom
  6. Swarm Agent Architecture

Have you ever been in a place where you have built a multi-agent system with few agents and few tools? As requirements grow bigger and bigger, more and more tools are coming into your systems, and agents have multiple tools, sometimes as many as 10 tools.

This can lead agents to be confused on what tool to use; agents begin to make poor decisions on tool selection. At this point, it can really get frustrating. One quick solution is to look into your code and try to understand what the underlying architecture of your program is. This can only help if you truly understand your agent architecture and what the agents are to do, what tasks your agents are designed to do.

In this article, we'll go over a basic understanding of these multi-agent architectures and in the upcoming articles, we'll dive deep into each one specifically.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns
Architecture 1 of 6

Single Agent Architecture

In a single agent architecture, this is the simplest to understand. In this approach, we only have one agent with a host of tools and connected to an LLM. The agent then takes in a query and makes decisions on what tool to call using the LLM for reasoning.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns
Architecture 2 of 6

Supervisor Agent Architecture

In the supervisor architecture, we have one agent that has multiple other agents (sub-agents) under it. The supervisor, basically, you can think of it as the orchestrator in a church choir. It takes in queries, uses an LLM to reason over it and decide on what agents to delegate a task to or a sub-task to. It receives the input from these agents, reasons over it and decides whether to call another agent if needed or not, if not, it returns the final output.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns
Architecture 3 of 6

Hierarchical Agent Architecture

Sometimes, having only one supervisor that makes all the decisions and deciding on what agent to call, the agent can start to under-perform due to so many things it has to handle and be an expert at handling. In such cases, one common approach is create teams, where each team has its own supervisor, that supervisor is specialized in managing its own team of sub-agents. Basically breaking the graph into subgraphs, each sub-graph has its supervisor and sub-agents under that supervisor.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns
Architecture 4 of 6

Network Agent Architecture

Networking, I personally understand this with experiences from normal day life. In a normal life setting, you can talk to anyone and they can give you feedback. You can shoot a message to a person you admire on LinkedIn, or any girl/boy you like right? Same concept here, but now with agents, each agent can talk to any other agent in the whole collection.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns
Architecture 5 of 6

Custom Agent Architecture

In this architecture of agents, each agent can only communicate with selected sub agents and unlike networking where each agent can communicate with all other agents.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns
Architecture 6 of 6

Swarm Agent Architecture

A swarm agent architecture is a type of multi-agent system where specialized agents dynamically pass control to one another based on their areas of expertise, with the system maintaining memory of which agent was last active to ensure conversation continuity.

Conclusion

Congratulations for making it this far, in this article, we went over the theoretical understanding of multi-agent architectures. Powered with this knowledge, let's now dive into each individual project and understand the implementation from the code standpoint.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Introduction

Why monolithic agents don't scale

The world of software development has already learned this lesson: monolithic applications don't scale. Whether you're building a massive e-commerce platform or a complex AI application, relying on a single, all-in-one entity creates bottlenecks, increases debugging costs, and limits specialized performance.

The same principle applies to an AI agent. A single agent tasked with too many responsibilities becomes a "Jack of all trades, master of none." As the complexity of instructions increases, adherence to specific rules degrades, and error rates compound, leading to more and more "hallucinations." If your agent fails, you shouldn't have to tear down the entire prompt to find the bug.

Reliability comes from decentralization and specialization. Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) allow you to build the AI equivalent of a microservices architecture. By assigning specific roles (a Parser, a Critic, a Dispatcher) to individual agents, you build systems that are inherently more modular, testable, and reliable.

In this guide we'll be using the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) to illustrate 8 essential design patterns, from the Sequential Pipeline to the Human-in-the-loop design pattern, providing you with the concrete patterns and pseudocode you need to build production-grade agent teams.

📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 1 of 8

Sequential Pipeline Pattern (aka the assembly line)

Let's start with the bread and butter of agent workflows. Think of this pattern as a classic assembly line where Agent A finishes a task and hands the baton directly to Agent B. It is linear, deterministic, and refreshingly easy to debug because you always know exactly where the data came from.

This is your go-to architecture for data processing pipelines. In the example below, we see a flow for processing raw documents: a Parser Agent turns a raw PDF into text, an Extractor Agent pulls out structured data, and a Summarizer Agent generates the final synopsis.

In ADK, the SequentialAgent primitive handles the orchestration for you. The secret sauce here is state management: simply use the output_key to write to the shared session.state so the next agent in the chain knows exactly where to pick up the work.

Python 
# ADK Pseudocode
# Step 1: Parse the PDF
parser = LlmAgent(
    name="ParserAgent",
    instruction="Parse raw PDF and extract text.",
    tools=[PDFParser],
    output_key="raw_text"
)

# Step 2: Extract structured data
extractor = LlmAgent(
    name="ExtractorAgent",
    instruction="Extract structured data from {raw_text}.",
    tools=[RegexExtractor],
    output_key="structured_data"
)

# Step 3: Summarize
summarizer = LlmAgent(
    name="SummarizerAgent",
    instruction="Generate summary from {structured_data}.",
    tools=[SummaryEngine]
)

# Orchestrate the Assembly Line
pipeline = SequentialAgent(
    name="PDFProcessingPipeline",
    sub_agents=[parser, extractor, summarizer]
)
📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 2 of 8

Coordinator/Dispatcher Pattern (aka the concierge)

Sometimes you don't need a chain; you need a decision maker. In this pattern, a central, intelligent agent acts as a dispatcher. It analyzes the user's intent and routes the request to a specialist agent best suited for the job.

This is ideal for complex customer service bots where you might need to send a user to a "Billing" specialist for invoice issues versus a "Tech Support" specialist for troubleshooting.

This relies on LLM-driven delegation. You simply define a parent CoordinatorAgent and provide a list of specialist sub_agents. The ADK's AutoFlow mechanism takes care of the rest, transferring execution based on the descriptions you provide for the children.

Python 
# ADK Pseudocode
billing_specialist = LlmAgent(
    name="BillingSpecialist",
    description="Handles billing inquiries and invoices.",
    tools=[BillingSystemDB]
)

tech_support = LlmAgent(
    name="TechSupportSpecialist",
    description="Troubleshoots technical issues.",
    tools=[DiagnosticTool]
)

# The Coordinator (Dispatcher)
coordinator = LlmAgent(
    name="CoordinatorAgent",
    # The instructions guide the routing logic
    instruction="Analyze user intent. Route billing issues to BillingSpecialist and bugs to TechSupportSpecialist.",
    sub_agents=[billing_specialist, tech_support]
)
📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 3 of 8

Parallel Fan-Out/Gather Pattern (aka the octopus)

Speed matters. If you have tasks that don't depend on each other, why run them one by one? In this pattern, multiple agents execute tasks simultaneously to reduce latency or gain diverse perspectives. Their outputs are then aggregated by a final "synthesizer" agent .

This is ideal for something like Automated Code Review. Instead of running checks sequentially, you can spawn a "Security Auditor," a "Style Enforcer," and a "Performance Analyst" to review a Pull Request simultaneously. Once they finish, a "Synthesizer" agent combines their feedback into a single, cohesive review comment.

The ParallelAgent in ADK should be used to run sub-agents simultaneously. Be aware that although these agents operate in separate execution threads, they share the session state. To prevent race conditions, make sure each agent writes its data to a unique key.

Python 
# ADK Pseudocode

# Define parallel workers
security_scanner = LlmAgent(
    name="SecurityAuditor",
    instruction="Check for vulnerabilities like injection attacks.",
    output_key="security_report"
)

style_checker = LlmAgent(
    name="StyleEnforcer",
    instruction="Check for PEP8 compliance and formatting issues.",
    output_key="style_report"
)

complexity_analyzer = LlmAgent(
    name="PerformanceAnalyst",
    instruction="Analyze time complexity and resource usage.",
    output_key="performance_report"
)

# Fan-out (The Swarm)
parallel_reviews = ParallelAgent(
    name="CodeReviewSwarm",
    sub_agents=[security_scanner, style_checker, complexity_analyzer]
)

# Gather/Synthesize
pr_summarizer = LlmAgent(
    name="PRSummarizer",
    instruction="Create a consolidated Pull Request review using {security_report}, {style_report}, and {performance_report}."
)

# Wrap in a sequence
workflow = SequentialAgent(sub_agents=[parallel_reviews, pr_summarizer])
📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 4 of 8

Hierarchical Decomposition (aka the russian doll)

Sometimes a task is too big for one agent context window. High-level agents can break down complex goals into sub-tasks and delegate them. Unlike the routing pattern, the parent agent might delegate just part of a task and wait for the result to continue its own reasoning.

In this diagram, we see a ReportWriter that doesn't do the research itself. It delegates to a ResearchAssistant, which in turn manages WebSearch and Summarizer tools.

You can treat a sub-agent as a tool here. By wrapping an agent in AgentTool, the parent agent can call it explicitly, effectively treating the sub-agent's entire workflow as a single function call.

Python 
# ADK Pseudocode
# Level 3: Tool Agents
web_searcher = LlmAgent(name="WebSearchAgent", description="Searches web for facts.")
summarizer = LlmAgent(name="SummarizerAgent", description="Condenses text.")

# Level 2: Coordinator Agent
research_assistant = LlmAgent(
    name="ResearchAssistant",
    description="Finds and summarizes info.",
    # Coordinator manages the tool agents
    sub_agents=[web_searcher, summarizer]
)

# Level 1: Top-Level Agent
report_writer = LlmAgent(
    name="ReportWriter",
    instruction="Write a comprehensive report on AI trends. Use the ResearchAssistant to gather info.",
    # Wrap the sub-agent hierarchy as a tool for the parent
    tools=[AgentTool(research_assistant)]
)
📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 5 of 8

Generator and Critic (aka the editor's desk)

Generating high-quality, reliable output often requires a second pair of eyes. In this pattern, you separate the creation of content from the validation of content. One agent acts as the Generator, producing a draft, while a second agent acts as the Critic, reviewing it against specific, hard-coded criteria or logical checks.

This architecture is distinct because of its conditional looping. If the review passes, the loop breaks, and the content is finalized. If it fails, specific feedback is routed back to the Generator to produce a compliant draft. This is incredibly useful for code generation that needs syntax checking or content creation requiring compliance review.

To implement this in ADK, you separate concerns into two specific primitives: a SequentialAgent that manages the draft-and-review interaction, and a parent LoopAgent that enforces the quality gate and exit condition.

Python 
# ADK Pseudocode

# The Generator
generator = LlmAgent(
    name="Generator",
    instruction="Generate a SQL query. If you receive {feedback}, fix the errors and generate again.",
    output_key="draft"
)

# The Critic
critic = LlmAgent(
    name="Critic",
    instruction="Check if {draft} is valid SQL. If correct, output 'PASS'. If not, output error details.",
    output_key="feedback"
)

# The Loop
loop = LoopAgent(
    name="ValidationLoop",
    sub_agents=[generator, critic],
    condition_key="feedback",
    exit_condition="PASS"
)
📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 6 of 8

Iterative Refinement (aka the sculptor)

Great work rarely happens in a single draft. Just like a human writer needs to revise, polish, and edit, sometimes your agents need a few attempts to get an answer exactly right. In this pattern, agents enter a cycle of generating, critiquing, and refining until the output meets a specific quality threshold.

Unlike the Generator and Critic pattern, which focuses on correctness (Pass/Fail), this pattern focuses on qualitative improvement. A Generator creates a rough draft, a Critique Agent provides optimization notes, and a Refinement Agent polishes the output based on those notes

This pattern is implemented using the LoopAgent. A critical component here is the exit mechanism. While you can set a hard limit using max_iterations, ADK also allows agents to signal early completion. An agent can trigger an exit by signaling escalate=True within its EventActions if the quality threshold is met before the maximum iterations are reached.

Python 
# ADK Pseudocode

# Generator
generator = LlmAgent(
    name="Generator",
    instruction="Generate an initial rough draft.",
    output_key="current_draft"
)

# Critique Agent
critic = LlmAgent(
    name="Critic",
    instruction="Review {current_draft}. List ways to optimize it for performance.",
    output_key="critique_notes"
)

# Refiner Agent
refiner = LlmAgent(
    name="Refiner",
    instruction="Read {current_draft} and {critique_notes}. Rewrite the draft to be more efficient.",
    output_key="current_draft" # Overwrites the draft with better version
)

# The Loop (Critique -> Refine)
loop = LoopAgent(
    name="RefinementLoop",
    max_iterations=3,
    sub_agents=[critic, refiner]
)

# Complete Workflow
workflow = SequentialAgent(sub_agents=[generator, loop])
📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 7 of 8

Human-in-the-loop (the human safety net)

AI Agents are powerful, but sometimes you need a human in the driver's seat for critical decision-making. In this model, agents handle the groundwork, but a human must authorize high-stakes actions - specifically those that are irreversible or carry significant consequences. This includes executing financial transactions, deploying code to production, or taking action based on sensitive data (as opposed to merely processing it), ensuring safety and accountability.

The diagram shows a Transaction Agent processing routine work. When a high-stakes check is needed, it calls an ApprovalTool Agent, which pauses execution and waits for a Human Reviewer to say "Yes" or "No."

ADK allows you to implement this via custom tools. An agent can call an approval_tool which pauses execution or triggers an external system to request human intervention.

Python 
# ADK Pseudocode
transaction_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="TransactionAgent",
    instruction="Handle routine processing. If high stakes, call ApprovalTool.",
    tools=[ApprovalTool]
)

approval_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="ApprovalToolAgent",
    instruction="Pause execution and request human input."
)

workflow = SequentialAgent(sub_agents=[transaction_agent, approval_agent])
📚 Library › Agentic AI & LLM Engineering › Developer's Guide to Multi-Agent Patterns in ADK
Pattern 8 of 8

Composite patterns (the mix-and-match)

Real-world enterprise applications rarely fit into a single box. You will likely combine these patterns to build production-grade applications.

For example, a robust Customer Support system might use a Coordinator to route requests. If the user has a technical issue, that branch might trigger a Parallel search of documentation and user history. The final answer might then go through a Generator and Critic loop to ensure tone consistency before being sent to the user.

A few pro-tips before you start

  • State management is vital: In ADK, session.state is your whiteboard. Use descriptive keys when using output_key so downstream agents know exactly what they are reading.
  • Clear descriptions: When using routing, the description field of your sub-agents is effectively your API documentation for the LLM. Be precise.
  • Start simple: Do not build a nested loop system on day one. Start with a sequential chain, debug it, and then add complexity.

Background

Background & The Operational Strain

Dr. Maya Kapoor, a 32-year-old primary care physician in Mumbai, has built her reputation on personalized patient care and her guiding principle: "do no harm." Her small neighborhood clinic has experienced explosive growth—driven by her reputation for quality, affordability, and ethics. Families across the city now flock to her for accurate treatment delivered with empathy and trust.

Now Maya dreams of building a multi-speciality super-hospital that scales her vision of care, affordability, and ethics across cardiology, oncology, orthopedics, maternal health, and more.

The Operational Strain

Maya's clinic had become a victim of its own success. On most mornings, the waiting room was overflowing, patients lining up outside before dawn in hopes of securing an appointment. What had started as a small neighborhood practice now carried the weight of hundreds of families' expectations every single day. Yet beneath this outward success, Maya saw cracks widening in the foundation:

Inconsistent care & weak governance. Each doctor in her clinic carried their own "style" of diagnosis and treatment. While some were thorough and empathetic, others rushed through consultations, cutting corners under pressure. Senior physicians bristled at the idea of being told how to practice medicine, and Maya found herself in a constant tug-of-war: how do you preserve professional autonomy while enforcing consistency in care?

High staff attrition. Nurses and junior doctors rarely stayed long. Tempted away by larger hospitals offering higher salaries and clearer career ladders, they left just as they began to understand the culture Maya was trying to build. For every departure, Maya had to start from scratch—recruit, retrain, and rebuild team cohesion.

Low salaries leading to frequent mistakes. The economics of affordable care meant salaries were modest. For staff juggling double shifts, exhaustion blurred their judgment. Prescriptions were sometimes entered incorrectly; lab reports were misplaced; routine procedures occasionally overlooked. Each mistake—small on its own—carried the weight of Maya's deepest fear: harm done to a patient in her name.

Expensive training cycles. With staff turnover so high, Maya's investment in training felt like pouring water into a sieve. Hours of workshops, mentorship, and hands-on shadowing were lost the moment a nurse or junior doctor walked out the door. The process was not only costly in rupees but emotionally draining—how many times could she re-teach the same basics before losing faith?

Revenue vs. reputation tension. Every day was a balancing act. More patients meant more revenue, a chance to stabilize the hospital's fragile finances. The average billing per patient is approximately ₹800. But the more patients her doctors tried to see, the more rushed the consultations became, and the more Maya worried that her reputation—the very thing that drew people to her—was slipping through her fingers. To expand meant risking what she valued most: the trust and safety of her patients.

📚 Library › AI in the Real World: Case Studies › From Clinic to Super-Speciality
Research

Learning from India's Leaders

Before committing to her hospital, Maya studied Indian institutions that embody affordability, quality, and ethics at scale. She discovered that many of her operational nightmares had already been addressed—albeit in the narrower domain of eye care—by pioneers like L V Prasad Eye Institute (LVPEI) and Sankara Nethralaya (SN).

L V Prasad Eye Institute (LVPEI). LVPEI runs a pyramidal care model that pushes basic care into the community while reserving complex cases for tertiary and quaternary centers. This structure reduces bottlenecks, ensures standardization, and makes care more consistent across millions of patients. Staff training is baked into the system—each layer of the pyramid functions as both a service provider and a training center, solving the problem of expensive and repetitive training cycles Maya dreads.

Attrition is minimized because LVPEI offers clear career ladders and mentorship opportunities, while oversight mechanisms ensure that low-salaried staff are supported by strong protocols, reducing errors. Financial sustainability comes through cross-subsidization: paying patients cover more than half of the 2 million outpatients treated annually, keeping care free or low-cost for those who need it.

Sankara Nethralaya (SN). SN tackles governance and culture differently. Rather than layering strict oversight, it has built a deep institutional ethos of compassion, teamwork, and ethical responsibility. Doctors and staff know that every patient—rich or poor—must receive the same quality of care, eliminating the "two-tier" risk Maya fears in her model. This shared culture helps manage inconsistency and governance challenges, even as patient numbers climb.

To combat attrition and extend its reach, SN leverages teleophthalmology and mobile surgical units, allowing teams to deliver standardized care in rural areas while giving staff meaningful community-facing work that improves retention. Subsidized surgeries (₹1,500–₹2,000 for cataracts) ensure affordability without compromising outcomes, reinforcing reputation even at scale.

Together, these institutions show Maya that her operational strains are not insurmountable:

  • Standardization can come from system design (LVPEI's pyramid) or culture (SN's compassion).
  • Attrition can be addressed by embedding education and mission-driven work.
  • Errors at lower salary levels can be minimized through strong protocols or shared values.
  • Training costs can be reduced by making every care tier a training platform.
  • Revenue vs. reputation can be balanced through cross-subsidization and equal-quality commitments.

For discussion

Student Discussion Questions

  1. Which user problems is AI uniquely positioned to solve, and why?
    • Which challenges (attrition, low salaries, training costs, governance, errors, volume vs. quality) align with AI's strengths?
    • Which issues are best solved by human systems (e.g., LVPEI training, SN compassion culture)?
  2. How can we augment human capabilities in addition to automating tasks? Is this practical?
    • What tasks should be automated (billing, records) vs augmented (decision-support, onboarding aids, safety alerts)?
    • How might augmentation reduce mistakes and training costs?
  3. How can we ensure our reward function optimizes AI for the right thing?
    • If AI is rewarded for speed or cost savings alone, quality may suffer. Which ethical metrics—zero avoidable harm, equitable access, standardized governance, patient trust—should define AI success?
    • How do LVPEI and SN's emphasis on equity and outcomes inform this?
  4. Financial Exercise:
    Suppose Maya treats 200,000 patients/year, with 40% paying and 60% subsidized. Example: cardiac bypass at ₹2,50,000 vs subsidized ₹30,000; knee replacement at ₹1,50,000 vs subsidized ₹20,000.

    Calculate

    • (a) gross revenue;
    • (b) net subsidy coverage after subtracting AI overhead (₹742–1,415 per patient);
    • (c) which AI solutions should Maya prioritize for max quality gains at minimum financial burden?

Closing thoughts

Final Thoughts

Maya wants India's first AI-enabled, values-driven multi-speciality hospital. Her challenge: target AI where it maximizes safety/quality while avoiding solutions that double per-patient costs. Selective, staged adoption is essential to preserve affordability.

The AI-Enabled Service Agent: Scaling Without Losing the Customer

Case Study DS-005 · Meera Joshi must cut costs and raise CSAT with AI, on a capped budget, without breaking her team

My second case study in this book. A fast-growing customer support org is drowning in disconnected systems and burnout. Leadership wants AI as the fix — but with a hard budget cap, a 9-month deadline, and $100M in contracts riding on it, this is a change-management and ROI problem as much as a technical one.

Background

HelixServe Technologies

Company: HelixServe Technologies

  • A Silicon Valley darling, HelixServe just closed a $600M Series F funding round.
  • Known for its lightning-fast growth in managing customer operations for Fortune 500 clients, HelixServe is scaling at breakneck speed.
  • With investors demanding aggressive expansion and the CEO determined not to repeat the mistakes of startups that scaled recklessly and lost their customer focus, the spotlight has turned to the one function that touches every client daily: customer support.

At the center of this storm is Meera Joshi, the Head of Customer Support.

Meera leads a global team of 600 agents across four continents. Her mandate: keep customers happy while managing the operational chaos of rapid scaling. But the reality on the ground is brutal. Agents like Taniya Sharma, a 25-year-old support associate in Mumbai, start their day juggling ten disconnected systems—customer history, FAQs, billing, refunds, compliance checks, live chat, escalation tracking, reporting dashboards—none of which talk to each other.

The result? Every simple query becomes a scavenger hunt.

  • Average Handling Time (AHT) has ballooned from 3 minutes to 7 minutes.
  • Customer Satisfaction (CSAT) scores have dropped from 8.2/10 to 6.1/10.
  • High call volumes, over 1,500 per day during peak season, created $40,000 in excess annual operating costs.
  • Attrition has spiked to 28%, with agents burned out and disengaged.

Meera knows this is unsustainable. The company is bleeding $4.2M annually in excess operating costs just to keep up with inefficiencies.

And yet, she also knows that customer support is the company's frontline brand experience. If customers feel abandoned in their moments of frustration, all the $600M in funding won't matter.

📚 Library › AI in the Real World: Case Studies › The AI-Enabled Service Agent
Turning point

The Catalyst

The crisis came to a head during HelixServe's Q3 board meeting.

  • Investors applauded the company's rapid growth but warned against the dangers of scaling without operational discipline.
"Remember WebWave?" one VC snapped. "They scaled too fast, lost their customer focus, and collapsed. Don't be next."
  • The CEO, a former operator who had seen startups implode from chaos, made it clear:
"We will not die of our own success. If scaling means confusing our customers, we won't scale at all."
  • The CFO's Office raised alarms about scalability: with query volumes projected to double during peak seasons, operational costs could spiral out of control. Without automation, support costs would eat into margins and threaten profitability.

Caught in the middle, Meera Joshi faced impossible math:

  • Improve customer satisfaction.
  • Reduce costs.
  • Scale operations for hypergrowth.

And she had to do all this without breaking the fragile human engine—her support team.

📚 Library › AI in the Real World: Case Studies › The AI-Enabled Service Agent
The dilemma

The Challenge

HelixServe's leadership turned to AI as the savior.

For Meera, this felt like both a lifeline and a gamble.

AI promised to:

  • Handle repetitive FAQs, freeing agents for complex cases.
  • Recommend real-time answers, reducing hold times.
  • Predict intent behind vague queries, cutting down back-and-forth.

But she wonders: How will AI adoption impact her role and career path? Will it create opportunities to upskill and focus on higher-value work, or will her contribution be undervalued as automation expands?

From the company's perspective:

  • Promise: Faster responses, improved CSAT, reduced costs.
  • Cost: AI credits may be inexpensive ($2,500 annually), but licenses, integrations, and training bring total costs closer to $13,500 annually.
  • Risk: Poorly trained AI could frustrate customers even more, leading to churn and reputational damage. Integrating AI into legacy systems could trigger weeks of downtime, just as new enterprise clients were onboarding.

The leadership team must weigh efficiency, customer trust, and employee morale carefully.

📚 Library › AI in the Real World: Case Studies › The AI-Enabled Service Agent
Who's in the room

Stakeholder Perspectives

Meera Joshi, Head of Customer Support (Protagonist). Under relentless pressure to raise CSAT while reducing AHT, she knows her credibility with the CEO and board hinges on this transformation. A failed rollout could end her career and fracture her team's already fragile morale.

Customer Support Agents (Taniya & peers). Overworked, demoralized, and fearful of AI replacing their roles. They worry that "efficiency" will come at the cost of empathy.

The Office of the CFO. Focused on scalability and cost discipline. Their models show that without automation, operating costs will balloon as query volumes double, threatening profitability even with the new funding.

IT & Engineering. Tasked with integration across legacy systems while meeting compliance standards. Scarred by past failed software rollouts, they demand airtight specifications before committing.

Compliance & Risk Officers. Worried about data privacy, regulatory breaches, and bias in AI decision-making.

The CEO. Obsessed with preventing "the death spiral of scale." He sees AI as the only way to grow without drowning in chaos—but insists it must improve customer trust, not erode it.

📚 Library › AI in the Real World: Case Studies › The AI-Enabled Service Agent
The numbers

The Mandate, Goal & Business Details

The executive board issued a non-negotiable mandate:

  • Deploy AI within 9 months.
  • Annual budget capped at $50,000, inclusive of licenses, deployment, integration, recurring maintenance, and fine tuning costs.
  • Tied to revenue: success will directly influence the renewal of ~$100M in enterprise contracts.

Failure would mean wasted investment, collapsing morale among support staff, erosion of customer trust, and a potential loss of credibility for HelixServe in the Valley—the kind of stumble that once derailed unicorns like WebWave.

The Goal (and Risk). If successful, this approach could improve CSAT back to 9/10, reduce agent turnover (currently 28%) by making the job less stressful, deliver a net ROI of ~$9,000 annually after costs, scale ROI at a compound rate of ~40% annually, and position the company as an AI-first service provider. But if implementation fails, the organization risks wasted investment, lower employee morale, further erosion of customer trust, and HelixServe could become another cautionary tale of a unicorn undone by its own growth.

For discussion

Discussion Questions

1. User Experience & Empathy

  • How can AI enhance Taniya's role instead of replacing it?
  • How should the system ensure customers still feel cared for when AI is the first touchpoint?

2. Business ROI & Cost-Benefit

  • Given the projected savings and AI costs, how should leadership evaluate whether the ROI is strong enough to justify the investment?
  • Beyond financial ROI, what qualitative or long-term benefits should the company measure (e.g., customer trust, employee retention, competitive advantage)?

3. Technology & Implementation

  • What challenges exist in training AI to understand diverse customer queries?
  • How can the company ensure fairness, accuracy, and data privacy in AI responses?

4. Change Management & Adoption

  • How should the company address Taniya's concerns about evolving responsibilities?
  • What training or support will help agents adapt to working alongside AI?

5. Financial ROI & Strategy

  • Beyond the immediate ROI, what longer-term benefits (e.g., reduced turnover, brand reputation) should leadership consider?
  • How should the company justify AI investment to skeptical stakeholders?

6. Scaling & Sustainability

  • If query volumes double during peak season, how should the company plan for AI scaling costs?
  • What risks exist if competitors adopt AI faster and achieve greater efficiency?
